metadata.title: Regret-based continuous-time dynamics
metadata.registry_mismatch_note: Registry metadata.json lists this paper as Hart & Mas-Colell (2000), 'A Simple Adaptive Procedure Leading to Correlated Equilibrium' (Econometrica 68:1127-1150), but the PDF/text actually contains Hart & Mas-Colell (2003), 'Regret-based continuous-time dynamics' (Games and Economic Behavior 45:375-394). Extraction reflects the actual PDF content (the 2003 continuous-time companion paper). The 2000 paper is cited in the references as 'Hart and Mas-Colell, 2000'.

nodes.name: $N$-person game in strategic form
nodes.statement: An $N$-person game $\Gamma$ consists of a finite set $N$ of players, a finite action set $S^i$ for each $i \in N$, payoff functions $u^i : S \to \mathbb{R}$ on $S := \prod_{i \in N} S^i$, with payoff bound $|u^i(s)| \le M$.
nodes.statement_clean: Standard finite strategic-form game with bounded payoffs.

nodes.name: Mixed action and joint distribution
nodes.statement: A mixed action is $x^i \in \Delta(S^i)$; a joint distribution is $z \in \Delta(S)$ with marginals $z^i(s^i) = \sum_{s^{-i}} z(s^i, s^{-i})$. $z$ is independent (a product measure) if $z(s) = \prod_{i} z^i(s^i)$.
nodes.statement_clean: Probability distributions on pure-action profiles, with marginals and the product (independence) condition.

nodes.name: Continuous-time replicator-style dynamics
nodes.statement: $\dot z(t) = \frac{1}{t}\bigl(q(t) - z(t)\bigr)$, where $q(t) \in \Delta(S)$ is the joint play at time $t$ and $z(t)$ is the time-average joint play, with initial $z(1) \in \Delta(S)$.
nodes.statement_clean: ODE for the time-average joint play, derived as the continuous limit of $z_t = z_{t-1} + (1/t)(\mathbf{1}_{s_t} - z_{t-1})$.

nodes.name: Regret vector $D^i(z)$
nodes.statement: For a joint distribution $z \in \Delta(S)$, the regret of player $i$ for action $k$ is $D^i_k(z) := u^i(k, z^{-i}) - u^i(z)$, and $D^i(z) := (D^i_k(z))_{k \in S^i}$.
nodes.statement_clean: How much $i$'s payoff would improve by always playing $k$ instead, given the marginal of others.

nodes.name: Hannan set $H$
nodes.statement: $H := \{z \in \Delta(S) : u^i(z) \ge \max_{k \in S^i} u^i(k, z^{-i}) \text{ for all } i \in N\}$, equivalently $D^i(z) \le 0$ for all $i$.
nodes.statement_clean: Joint distributions where every player's payoff is at least the best-reply payoff against the marginal of the others.

nodes.name: Properties of the Hannan set
nodes.statement: $H$ is a convex polytope, contains all correlated equilibria (hence all Nash equilibria), and an independent $z$ lies in $H$ iff $z$ is a Nash equilibrium.
nodes.statement_clean: Three structural facts about $H$.

nodes.name: Potential function $P$
nodes.statement:
A function $P : \mathbb{R}^m 	o \mathbb{R}$ is a potential if (P1) $P$ is $C^1$ with $P(x) > 0$ for $x 
otin \mathbb{R}^m_-$ and $P(x) = 0$ on $\mathbb{R}^m_-$; (P2) $
abla P(x) \ge 0$ and $
abla P(x) \cdot x > 0$ off $\mathbb{R}^m_-$; (P3) $P(x) = P([x]_+)$; (P4) $ho_1 P(x) \le 
abla P(x) \cdot x \le ho_2 P(x)$ for some $0 < ho_1 \le ho_2 < \infty$.
nodes.statement_clean: Smooth nonnegative function vanishing on the negative orthant with controlled local returns to scale; e.g., $P(x) = \|[x]_+\|_p^p$.

nodes.name: Normalized gradient $\widehat{\nabla} P$
nodes.statement:
$\widehat{
abla} P(x) := 
abla P(x) / \|
abla P(x)\| \in \Delta(m)$ for $x 
otin \mathbb{R}^m_-$.
nodes.statement_clean: Probability vector obtained by $\ell^1$-normalizing the gradient.

nodes.name: Regret-based strategy ($P^i$-strategy)
nodes.statement: Player $i$ plays a $P^i$-strategy if there exists a potential $P^i$ on $\mathbb{R}^{S^i}$ such that $q^i(t) = \widehat{\nabla} P^i(D^i(z(t)))$ whenever $D^i(z(t)) \notin \mathbb{R}^{S^i}_-$.
nodes.statement_clean: Mixed play proportional to the gradient of a potential evaluated at the current regret vector (regret-matching is the special case $P(x) = \|[x]_+\|_2^2$).

nodes.name: Invariance under utility transformations
nodes.statement: The class of regret-based strategies of $i$ is invariant under $\tilde u^i(s) := \alpha u^i(s) + v(s^{-i})$ for $\alpha > 0$ (and a corresponding rescaling of $P^i$).
nodes.statement_clean: Best-reply-preserving transformations leave the strategy class invariant.

nodes.name: Vanishing regret under regret-based strategies
nodes.statement: If $z(t)$ solves (2.1) and player $i$ plays a $P^i$-strategy (3.2), then $\lim_{t \to \infty} D^i_k(z(t)) \le 0$ for every $k \in S^i$.
nodes.statement_clean: Regret-based play drives every component of $i$'s regret vector to be at most zero in the limit.
assumptions: Player $i$ plays a regret-based strategy (3.2) with potential $P^i$ satisfying (P1)-(P4)
$q^{-i}(t)$ is arbitrary (other players may even correlate, but $q^{-i}$ is independent of $q^i$)

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.1 (Lyapunov via $\pi^i = P^i(D^i(z))$)
nodes.statement: Rescale time so that $\dot z = q - z$, set $\pi^i(z) := P^i(D^i(z))$, derive $q^i \cdot \dot D^i = -q^i \cdot D^i$, hence $\dot \pi^i = -\nabla P^i(D^i) \cdot D^i < 0$ off $\mathbb{R}^{S^i}_-$ (by P2); $\pi^i$ is a strict Lyapunov function so $\pi^i \to 0$.
nodes.statement_clean: Define $\pi^i := P^i(D^i(z))$ and show it is a strict Lyapunov function for the dynamics.

nodes.name: Time rescaling and regret derivative
nodes.statement: Take $\tilde t = \exp(t)$ so $\dot z = q - z$. Then $\dot D^i_k(z) = u^i(k \times q^{-i}) - u^i(q^i, q^{-i}) - D^i_k(z)$.

nodes.name: Identity $q^i \cdot \dot D^i = -q^i \cdot D^i$
nodes.statement: Multiplying the regret derivative by $q^i_k$ and summing over $k \in S^i$ gives $q^i \cdot \dot D^i(z) = -q^i \cdot D^i(z)$ (eq.\ (3.3)); the $u^i(k, q^{-i})$ terms collapse against $q^i$.

nodes.name: Lyapunov derivative for $\pi^i$
nodes.statement:
With $\pi^i := P^i(D^i(z))$, $\dot \pi^i = 
abla P^i(D^i) \cdot \dot D^i = \|
abla P^i(D^i)\|\, q^i \cdot \dot D^i = -
abla P^i(D^i) \cdot D^i$, using (3.2) and step 2.

nodes.name: Conclude $\pi^i \to 0$ via (P2)
nodes.statement: By (P2), $\dot \pi^i < 0$ whenever $D^i(z) \notin \mathbb{R}^{S^i}_-$, so $\pi^i$ is a strict Lyapunov function and $\pi^i(z(t)) \to 0$, which implies $D^i(z(t)) \to \mathbb{R}^{S^i}_-$.

nodes.name: Convergence to the Hannan set
nodes.statement: If all players play regret-based strategies, then $z(t)$ converges as $t \to \infty$ to the Hannan set $H$ (i.e., $\mathrm{dist}(z(t), H) \to 0$).
nodes.statement_clean: Joint regret-based play converges (set-wise) to $H$.
assumptions: Every player $i \in N$ uses a regret-based strategy (3.2)

nodes.name: Persistence of positive regret
nodes.statement: If $D^i(z(t_0)) \notin \mathbb{R}^{S^i}_-$ then $D^i(z(t)) \notin \mathbb{R}^{S^i}_-$ for all $t \ge t_0$.
nodes.statement_clean: Once positive regret appears, it never vanishes (regret only converges to $0$ in the limit).

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.3 (lower exponential bound on $\pi^i$)
nodes.statement: From (3.4) and (P3) (more precisely (P4)) one gets $\dot \pi^i \ge -\rho_2 \pi^i$, hence $\pi^i(t) \ge e^{-\rho_2 (t-t_0)} \pi^i(t_0) > 0$ for all $t > t_0$.
nodes.statement_clean: Integrate the differential inequality $\dot \pi^i \ge -\rho_2 \pi^i$.

nodes.name: Hannan-set + product-payoff implies Nash (two-person)
nodes.statement: In a two-person game, if $z \in H$ and $u^i(z) = u^i(z^1, z^2)$ for $i = 1, 2$ (eq.\ (4.2)), then $(z^1, z^2)$ is a Nash equilibrium.
nodes.statement_clean: When the Hannan-set payoff equals the product-marginal payoff, the marginals form a Nash equilibrium.
conclusions: $(z^1, z^2)$ is a Nash equilibrium of $\Gamma$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.1 (chain of inequalities)
nodes.statement: If $z \in H$ then $u^i(k^i, z^j) \le u^i(z) = u^i(z^1, z^2)$ for all $k^i \in S^i$, which is exactly the Nash inequality for the marginals.
nodes.statement_clean: One-line argument combining the Hannan inequality with the assumed equality.

nodes.name: Convergence to Nash in two-person zero-sum games
nodes.statement: In a two-person zero-sum game, if both players use regret-based strategies, then $(z^1(t), z^2(t))$ converges to the set of Nash equilibria, and both $u(z(t))$ and $u(z^1(t), z^2(t))$ converge to the minimax value $v$.
nodes.statement_clean: Regret-based play in zero-sum games converges to the value and to Nash strategies.
assumptions: $\Gamma$ is a two-person zero-sum game with $u^1 = u$, $u^2 = -u$
conclusions: $u(z(t)) \to v$ and $u(z^1(t), z^2(t)) \to v$ where $v$ is the minimax value

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.2
nodes.statement: Inequalities (4.1) for both players force the equalities (4.2); apply Theorem 3.1 (regrets vanish) and Lemma 4.1.
nodes.statement_clean: Two-line corollary of $D^i \to (-\infty, 0]$ together with Lemma 4.1.

nodes.name: Coordinate bound by potential ($\max_k x_k \le c P(x)^{1/\rho_2}$)
nodes.statement: For every potential $P$ satisfying (P1)-(P4) and every $K > 0$ there exists $c > 0$ with $\max_k x_k \le c\, P(x)^{1/\rho_2}$ for all $x \in [-K, K]^m$.
nodes.statement_clean: On a bounded box, the largest coordinate is controlled by the potential up to a power.
conclusions: There exists $c > 0$ such that $\max_k x_k \le c\, P(x)^{1/\rho_2}$ for all $x \in [-K, K]^m$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.3
nodes.statement: WLOG $\rho_2 = 1$; for $x \ge 0$ show $f(\tau)/\tau$ is decreasing where $f(\tau) = P(\tau x)$, deduce $P(\tau x) \ge \tau P(x)$ for $\tau \le 1$, then dominate $P(x) \ge a x_1/K$ along axes; extend to general $x$ via (P3).
nodes.statement_clean: Use monotonicity of $\tau \mapsto P(\tau x)/\tau$ and the floor on $\{x \ge 0, \|x\| = K\}$.

nodes.name: Convergence to Nash in two-person potential games (with initial regret)
nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma$ be a two-person potential game with $u^1 = u^2 = u$. Assume initially $D^i(z(1)) \notin \mathbb{R}^{S^i}_-$ for $i = 1, 2$. If both players use regret-based strategies, then $(z^1(t), z^2(t))$ converges to the set of Nash equilibria, and there exists $\bar v$ with both $u(z(t)) \to \bar v$ and $u(z^1(t), z^2(t)) \to \bar v$.
nodes.statement_clean: Regret-based play in two-person potential games converges to a Nash payoff $\bar v$, provided each player has some positive regret at $t=1$.
assumptions: $\Gamma$ is a two-person potential game ($u^1 = u^2 = u$)
conclusions: There exists $\bar v$ with $u(z(t)) \to \bar v$ and $u(z^1(t), z^2(t)) \to \bar v$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.4 (Lyapunov $v = u(z^1, z^2) - \pi^1/\rho - \pi^2/\rho$)
nodes.statement: Build the Lyapunov-type quantity $v := u(z^1, z^2) - \pi^1/\rho - \pi^2/\rho$, show $\dot v > 0$, conclude $v \to \bar v$. Then use Lemma 4.5 on $f := 2u(z) - 2u(z^1, z^2) + \pi^1 + \pi^2$ to get $u(z) - u(z^1, z^2) \to 0$, finishing via Lemma 4.1.
nodes.statement_clean: Construct an increasing bounded auxiliary functional and use a Lipschitz-integrability lemma.

nodes.name: Persistence of positive regrets
nodes.statement: By Lemma 3.3, $\pi^i(t) > 0$ for all $t \ge 1$ since $D^i(z(1)) \notin \mathbb{R}^{S^i}_-$.

nodes.name: Differential inequality for $u(z^1, z^2)$
nodes.statement: After rescaling $\dot z = q - z$, expand $\dot u(z^1 \times z^2)$ and use $u(q^1, z^2) > u(z)$ (P2) to obtain $\dot u(z^1, z^2) > 2u(z) - 2u(z^1, z^2)$ (eq.\ (4.4)).

nodes.name: Bound $u(z^1, z^2) - u(z) \le \pi^1$
nodes.statement: Using (4.3): $u(k, z^2) - u(z) = D^1_k(z) \le P^1(D^1(z)) = \pi^1$ for all $k$, hence $u(z^1, z^2) - u(z) \le \pi^1$ (eq.\ (4.5)). Combined with (4.4) yields $\dot u(z^1, z^2) > -\pi^1 - \pi^2$ (eq.\ (4.6)).

nodes.name: Contraction $\dot \pi^i \le -\rho \pi^i$
nodes.statement: Combining (3.4) and (P3)/(P4): $\dot \pi^i \le -\rho \pi^i$ where $\rho := \min_i \rho_1^i$ (eq.\ (4.7)).

nodes.name: Increasing Lyapunov $v$ and limit $\bar v$
nodes.statement: Define $v := u(z^1, z^2) - \pi^1/\rho - \pi^2/\rho$. From (4.6) and (4.7) get $\dot v \ge \dot u(z^1, z^2) + \pi^1 + \pi^2 > 0$ (eq.\ (4.8)); $v$ is bounded so $v \to \bar v$, and $\pi^i \to 0$ gives $u(z^1, z^2) \to \bar v$.

nodes.name: Use Lemma 4.5 on $f$
nodes.statement: Set $f := 2u(z) - 2u(z^1, z^2) + \pi^1 + \pi^2 \ge 0$ (by (4.5)); $f$ is uniformly Lipschitz and $\int_0^\infty f\, dt$ is bounded by $\bar v$ via (4.4) and (4.8). Lemma 4.5 gives $f \to 0$, hence $u(z) - u(z^1, z^2) \to 0$. Apply Lemma 4.1 to conclude.

nodes.name: Lipschitz integrable function vanishes
nodes.statement: Let $f : \mathbb{R}_+ \to \mathbb{R}_+$ be non-negative and uniformly Lipschitz, with $\int_0^\infty f(t)\, dt < \infty$. Then $f(t) \to 0$.
nodes.statement_clean: A non-negative integrable Lipschitz function on the half-line tends to zero.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.5
nodes.statement: If $f(T) \ge 2\varepsilon$ then by Lipschitzness $f \ge \varepsilon$ on $[T, T + \varepsilon/L]$, so $\int_T^{T+\varepsilon/L} f\, dt \ge \varepsilon^2/L$. The integral being finite forces only finitely many such $T$.
nodes.statement_clean: Each big spike contributes a fixed positive area; finitely many fit in a finite total integral.

nodes.name: Two-person potential games for arbitrary initial conditions
nodes.statement: Theorem 4.4 holds for any initial $z(1)$ when each player uses the strategy (4.9): play a fixed $\bar y^i$ until the first $T^i$ with $\max_k D^i_k(z(t)) \ge 1/t$, then switch to $\widehat{\nabla} P^i(D^i)$.
nodes.statement_clean: By delaying the switch to regret-matching until some regret is non-negligible, convergence to Nash holds from any starting point.
assumptions: Both players use the modified strategy (4.9)
conclusions: $(z^1(t), z^2(t)) \to$ set of Nash equilibria of $\Gamma$ for any initial $z(1)$

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 4.6 (case split on whether both eventually regret-match)
nodes.statement: If after some $T$ both players are regret-matching, apply Theorem 4.4 starting at $T$. Otherwise some $i$ plays $\bar y^i$ forever; then $D^i(z(t)) \to \mathbb{R}^{S^i}_-$ and $z^i(t) \to \bar y^i$, so $z(t)$ becomes independent in the limit and Lemma 4.1 yields the conclusion.
nodes.statement_clean: Two cases: eventual switch (use Theorem 4.4) or perpetual fixed strategy (independence in the limit + Lemma 4.1).

nodes.name: Other classes of two-person games
nodes.statement: Smooth fictitious play converges to (approximate) Nash for games with a unique interior ESS and for supermodular games (Hofbauer-Sandholm 2002). General regret-based strategies converge to Nash in the first class (Hofbauer, personal communication 2002); the supermodular case is open.
nodes.statement_clean: Status of regret-based dynamics for ESS and supermodular two-person games.

nodes.name: Conditional regret $C^i_{jk}(z)$
nodes.statement: $C^i_{jk}(z) := \sum_{s^{-i} \in S^{-i}} [u^i(k, s^{-i}) - u^i(j, s^{-i})]\, z(j, s^{-i})$ for $j \ne k \in S^i$; $C^i(z) := (C^i_{jk}(z))_{(j,k) \in L}$ where $L := \{(j,k) \in S^i \times S^i : j \ne k\}$.
nodes.statement_clean: Conditional regret: change in $i$'s payoff if action $j$ had always been replaced by $k$.

nodes.name: Correlated equilibrium
nodes.statement: $z \in \Delta(S)$ is a correlated equilibrium iff $C^i(z) \le 0$ for all $i \in N$ (i.e., $C^i_{jk}(z) \le 0$ for all $i, j \ne k$).
nodes.statement_clean: Joint distribution where no player gains by deviating from a recommendation; characterized by non-positive conditional regrets.
nodes.origin_citation: Hart and Mas-Colell 2000 (cited for the characterization)

nodes.name: Conditional regret-based strategy
nodes.statement:
Player $i$ plays a conditional regret-based strategy if there exists a potential $P^i : \mathbb{R}^L 	o \mathbb{R}$ such that, when $C^i(z(t)) 
otin \mathbb{R}^L_-$, $\dot q^i_j(t) = \sum_{k 
e j}[
abla_{(k,j)} P^i(C^i(z(t)))\, q^i_k(t) - 
abla_{(j,k)} P^i(C^i(z(t)))\, q^i_j(t)]$ (eq.\ (5.2)).
nodes.statement_clean: Continuous-time Markov-process-style update for $q^i$ driven by partial derivatives of the conditional-regret potential.

nodes.name: $q^i$ stays in the simplex
nodes.statement: The dynamics (5.2) satisfy $\sum_j \dot q^i_j = 0$ and $\dot q^i_j \ge 0$ when $q^i_j = 0$, so $q^i(t) \in \Delta(S^i)$ for all $t$ if $q^i(1) \in \Delta(S^i)$. Speeds of $q$ (constant) and $z$ ($1/t$) differ.
nodes.statement_clean: Forward invariance of $\Delta(S^i)$ for the $q^i$-dynamics.

nodes.name: Vanishing conditional regret (per-player)
nodes.statement: If player $i$ plays a conditional regret-based strategy, then $\lim_{t \to \infty} \max_{j,k} C^i_{jk}(z(t)) \le 0$ for any play $q^{-i}(t)$ of the other players.
nodes.statement_clean: Conditional regret of $i$ vanishes regardless of how other players play (universally calibrated).
assumptions: Player $i$ plays a conditional regret-based strategy with potential $P^i$ satisfying (P1)-(P4)

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5.1
nodes.statement: Compute $\dot C^i_{jk}$ from (2.1); set $\pi := P^i(C^i(z))$ and bound $\dot \pi \le -\pi/t + (1/t) E$ where $E$ is a weighted average of expressions $E(s^{-i}) = \sum_j u(j, s^{-i})\, \dot q^i_j$. Then show $\dot q^i \to 0$ via Proposition B.1 (using (5.6) $\dot q^i = M_3 q^i (A - I)$ with $A(t)$ stochastic and Lipschitz of order $1/t$). Conclude $E \to 0$, hence $t\dot \pi + \pi \le E \to 0$ gives $\pi \to 0$.
nodes.statement_clean: Reduce to a continuous-time Markov ODE; invoke Proposition B.1 to get $\dot q^i \to 0$, then derive $\pi \to 0$.

nodes.name: Lyapunov-style inequality $\dot \pi \le -\pi/t + E/t$
nodes.statement: With $\pi := P^i(C^i(z))$ and $G := \nabla P^i(C^i(z))$, use (P4) ($\rho_1 = 1$ WLOG) to get $\dot \pi \le -\pi/t + (1/t)\sum_{s^{-i}} q^{-i}_{s^{-i}}\sum_{j,k} G_{jk}[u^i(k,s^{-i}) - u^i(j,s^{-i})] q^i_j$ (eq.\ (5.4)); rewrite the inner sum as $E(s^{-i}) = \sum_j u(j, s^{-i}) \dot q^i_j$.

nodes.name: Markov-process form $\dot q^i = M_3 q^i (A - I)$
nodes.statement:
Define $A_{jk} := G_{jk}/M_3$ for $j 
e k$ and $A_{jj} := 1 - \sum_{k 
e j} G_{kj}/M_3$ (with $M_3 := \max \|
abla P^i\|$); $A(t)$ is stochastic and (5.2) becomes $\dot q^i(t) = M_3 q^i(t)(A(t) - I)$ (eq.\ (5.6)). Lipschitz bound $\|A(t_2) - A(t_1)\| \le mKM_2(t_2 - t_1)/(M_3 t_1)$ from $\|G\|$ Lipschitzness and $\|\dot C^i\| \le M_2/t$.

nodes.name: Apply Proposition B.1 to obtain $\dot q^i \to 0$
nodes.statement: Proposition B.1 (with $t \to M_3 t$) yields $\dot q^i(t) \to 0$, so $E(s^{-i}) = \sum_j u(j, s^{-i})\dot q^i_j \to 0$.

nodes.name: Conclude $\pi \to 0$
nodes.statement: From $t\dot \pi + \pi \le E(t) \to 0$: for $\varepsilon > 0$ and $t$ large, $d(t\pi)/dt \le \varepsilon$, so $t\pi(t) \le t_0 \pi(t_0) + \varepsilon(t - t_0)$ and $\limsup \pi \le \varepsilon$.

nodes.name: Convergence to correlated equilibria
nodes.statement: If all players use conditional regret-based strategies, then $z(t)$ converges as $t \to \infty$ to the set of correlated equilibria of $\Gamma$.
nodes.statement_clean: Set-wise convergence to the correlated-equilibrium set under joint conditional regret-based play.
assumptions: Every player plays a conditional regret-based strategy

nodes.name: Universal calibration in continuous time
nodes.statement: Unlike the discrete-time case, the result for continuous time applies to each player separately (no assumption on $q^{-i}$ in Theorem 5.1); informally, the Cahn (2000) condition is satisfied automatically in the continuous limit.
nodes.statement_clean: Continuous-time conditional regret-based strategies are universally calibrated.

nodes.name: State space and informational requirements (Section 6 a-c)
nodes.statement: (a) The state space is $\Delta(\prod_i S^i)$, not $\prod_i \Delta(S^i)$, contrasting with Brown-von Neumann-Nash evolutionary dynamics. (b) Players need only record their own past play in addition to opponents'. (c) Stochastic-approximation derivations of discrete-time analogs may be feasible for Section 3 / Appendix C results but are challenging for Sections 4 and 5.
nodes.statement_clean: Discussion of state-space choice, information requirements, and discrete-time linkage.

nodes.name: Discrete-time convergence to Nash for two-person potential games
nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma$ be a two-person potential game with potentials satisfying (P1)-(P5). If both players use the discrete-time regret-based strategy (A.1), then with probability 1 $(z^1_t, z^2_t)$ converges to the set of Nash equilibria, and the average realized payoff $u(z_t)$ (and $u(z^1_t, z^2_t)$) converges to the set of Nash equilibrium payoffs.
nodes.statement_clean: Discrete-time analog of Theorem 4.4: regret-based play (with the empirical-distribution fallback when no regret) almost-surely converges to Nash.
assumptions: Both players use the discrete-time strategy (A.1)
conclusions: $u(z_t)$ and $u(z^1_t, z^2_t)$ converge to the set of Nash equilibrium payoffs (a.s.)

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem A.1 (five steps)
nodes.statement: Step 1: $\pi^i_t \to 0$ a.s. with $E[\pi^i_t \mid h_{t-1}] \le (1 - \rho/t)\pi^i_{t-1} + M_1/t^2$. Step 2: define $\alpha^i_{t-1} := u(q^i_t, z^j_{t-1}) - u(z^1_{t-1}, z^2_{t-1}) + \pi^i_{t-1}$ and show $\alpha^i_{t-1} \ge 0$ with the strict bound (A.3) when $\pi^i_{t-1} > 0$. Step 3: $v_t := u(z^1_t, z^2_t) - \pi_t/\rho - \sum_{r > t} M_2/r^2$ is a bounded submartingale, hence $u(z^1_t, z^2_t) \to v$ a.s. Step 4: $1_{\pi^1_t > 0}(u(z_t) - u(z^1_t, z^2_t)) \to 0$ via Lemma A.2 applied to $\beta_t = (t-1)\alpha_{t-1}/t^2$. Step 5: $1_{\pi^1_t = 0}(u(z_t) - u(z^1_t, z^2_t)) \to 0$ via Azuma's inequality and Borel-Cantelli. Combine via Lemma 4.1.
nodes.statement_clean: Lyapunov-submartingale argument with a Markov-difference (Azuma) treatment of the no-regret regime.

nodes.name: Step 1: recursion (A.2) and $\pi^i_t \to 0$
nodes.statement: Compute $E[d^1_t(k) - d^1_{t-1}(k) \mid h_{t-1}] = (1/t)[u(k, q^2_t) - u(q^1_t, q^2_t)] - d^1_{t-1}(k)/t$; using (P4), (P5) get $E[\pi^1_t \mid h_{t-1}] \le (1 - \rho/t)\pi^1_{t-1} + M_1/t^2$; deduce $\pi^i_t \to 0$ a.s.

nodes.name: Step 2: positivity of $\alpha^i_{t-1}$
nodes.statement: From (4.3) get $u(k, z^j_{t-1}) - u(z_{t-1}) \le \pi^i_{t-1}$; averaging gives $u(z^1_{t-1}, z^2_{t-1}) - u(z_{t-1}) \le \pi^i_{t-1}$. If $\pi^1_{t-1} > 0$ then $u(q^1_t, z^2_{t-1}) > u(z_{t-1})$ by (P2), giving (A.3).

nodes.name: Step 3: bounded submartingale $v_t$
nodes.statement: Compute $E[t^2 u(z^1_t, z^2_t) \mid h_{t-1}]$, combine with Step 1 to derive $E[v_t \mid h_{t-1}] \ge v_{t-1} + ((t-1)/t^2)\alpha_{t-1} \ge v_{t-1}$ (eq.\ (A.5)). $v_t$ is bounded; $v_t \to v$ a.s.; $u(z^1_t, z^2_t) \to v$.

nodes.name: Step 4: Lemma A.2 forces $\beta_t \to 0$
nodes.statement: $w_T := \sum_{t=1}^T (E[v_{t+1} \mid h_t] - v_t) \ge \sum_t \beta_t/t$ with $\beta_t = (t-1)\alpha_{t-1}/t^2$; $\sup_T E(w_T) < \infty$, so $\sum_t \beta_t/t < \infty$ a.s. (eq.\ (A.7)). Combined with $|\beta_t - \beta_{t-1}| \le M_3/t$ (eq.\ (A.8)), Lemma A.2 gives $\beta_t \to 0$, hence $\alpha_t \to 0$, finishing $1_{\pi^1 > 0}(u(z) - u(z^1, z^2)) \to 0$.

nodes.name: Step 5: Azuma + Borel-Cantelli for $\pi^1_t = 0$
nodes.statement: Set $X_t := t(u(z_t) - u(z^1_t, z^2_t))$, $Y_t := \gamma_{t-1}(X_t - X_{t-1})$ (martingale differences with $|Y_t| \le 4M$); Azuma yields $\Pr[\sum_{R+1}^t Y_\tau > t\varepsilon] < t \exp(-\delta t)$ (eq.\ (A.9)); Borel-Cantelli gives the bound a.s.; combine cases for $R(t)$ (either $R(t) \to \infty$ and use Step 4, or $R(t) = r_0$ eventually).

nodes.name: Conclude via Lemma 4.1
nodes.statement: Steps 4 and 5 give $u(z_t) \to v$ (the same limit as $u(z^1_t, z^2_t)$ from Step 3). By Lemma 4.1, every limit point of $(z^1_t, z^2_t)$ is a Nash equilibrium with payoff $v$.

nodes.name: Slowly-varying integrable sequence vanishes
nodes.statement: If $(\beta_t)$ is non-negative with $\sum_t \beta_t/t < \infty$ and $|\beta_t - \beta_{t-1}| \le M_3/t$, then $\beta_t \to 0$.
nodes.statement_clean: Discrete analog of Lemma 4.5 for sequences with $1/t$-bounded increments and convergent $\sum \beta_t/t$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A.2
nodes.statement: WLOG $M_3 = 1$. If $\beta_t \ge 2\varepsilon$ then for $t \le r \le t + \varepsilon t$, $\beta_r \ge \varepsilon$, and $\beta_r/r \ge \varepsilon/(2t)$, so $\sum_{t \le r \le t + \varepsilon t} \beta_r/r \ge \varepsilon^2/2 > 0$. By (A.7) only finitely many such $t$.
nodes.statement_clean: Each spike $\beta_t \ge 2\varepsilon$ contributes a fixed positive chunk to $\sum \beta_r/r$; finitely many fit.

nodes.name: Continuous-time Markov ODE: $\dot x \to 0$ for slowly-varying stochastic $A(t)$
nodes.statement: Let $A(t)$ be a stochastic $m \times m$ matrix for $t \ge 1$ with $\|A(t_2) - A(t_1)\| \le K(t_2 - t_1)/t_1$ for all $t_2 \ge t_1 \ge 1$. Consider $\dot x(t) = x(t)(A(t) - I)$ with $x(1) \in \Delta(m)$. Then $\dot x(t) \to 0$ as $t \to \infty$.
nodes.statement_clean: Continuous-time Markov ODE with slowly-changing transition matrix has vanishing derivative.
assumptions: For all $t \ge 1$, $A(t)$ is a stochastic $m \times m$ matrix

nodes.name: Uniform $1/\sqrt{t}$ bound on $e^{t(A-I)}(A - I)$
nodes.statement: There exists a universal constant $c$ such that $\|e^{t(A-I)}(A - I)\| \le c/\sqrt{t}$ for any stochastic matrix $A$ and any $t \ge 1$.
nodes.statement_clean: $O(t^{-1/2})$ uniform decay of $e^{t(A - I)}(A - I)$, independent of $A$ and $m$.
assumptions: $A$ is a stochastic matrix (arbitrary size $m \times m$)
conclusions: $\|e^{t(A - I)}(A - I)\| \le c/\sqrt{t}$ for a universal constant $c$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition B.2 (Stirling on telescopic sums)
nodes.statement: Expand $e^{t(A-I)}(A-I) = e^{-t}\sum_n \alpha_n A^n$ with $\alpha_n = t^{n-1}/(n-1)! - t^n/n!$; bound $\|A^n\| = 1$ ($A$ stochastic), and the telescopic split $\sum_n |\alpha_n| = 2 t^r/r!$ for $r := \lfloor t \rfloor$. Stirling gives $t^r/r! \sim e^t/\sqrt{2\pi t}$, yielding the $1/\sqrt{t}$ bound.
nodes.statement_clean: Series expansion of the matrix exponential plus Stirling's formula on the dominant term.

nodes.name: Continuity bound for two stochastic ODEs
nodes.statement: Let $A(t), B(t)$ be stochastic $m \times m$ matrices with $x, y$ solving $\dot x = x(A(t) - I)$, $\dot y = y(B(t) - I)$, $x(1), y(1) \in \Delta(m)$. Then $\|x(t) - y(t)\| \le \|x(1) - y(1)\| + \int_1^t \|A(\tau) - B(\tau)\|\, d\tau$.
nodes.statement_clean: Stability/Gronwall-type estimate for two Markov ODEs in continuous time.
assumptions: $x, y$ solve the corresponding ODEs starting in $\Delta(m)$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma B.3 (Gronwall via $z := e^{t-1} x$)
nodes.statement: Set $z(t) := e^{t-1} x(t)$, $w(t) := e^{t-1} y(t)$, then $\dot z = zA$, $\dot w = wB$. Apply Gronwall to $v := \|z - w\|$ using $\dot v \le v + e^{t-1}\|A - B\|$; integrate and divide by $e^{t-1}$.
nodes.statement_clean: Standard Gronwall trick after multiplying by $e^{t-1}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition B.1 (split into $T_0, T$ with $\alpha = 2/5$)
nodes.statement: Set $\alpha = 2/5$, $T_0 := T - T^\alpha$. Freeze $A(T_0)$ over $[T_0, T]$ to get $y$ via Proposition B.2: $\|\dot y(T)\| = O(T^{-\alpha/2})$. Use Lemma B.3 with $\|A(t) - A(T_0)\| = O(T^{\alpha-1})$ for $t \in [T_0, T]$ to get $\|x(T) - y(T)\| = O(T^{2\alpha-1})$. Combine: $\|\dot x(T)\| = O(T^{-\alpha/2}) + O(T^{2\alpha - 1}) = O(T^{-1/5})$.
nodes.statement_clean: Compare $x$ to a frozen-coefficient $y$ over a window of length $T^\alpha$, balance the two error terms.

nodes.name: Continuous-time generalized approachability
nodes.statement:
Let $C \subset \mathbb{R}^m$ be a closed convex approachable set, $P : \mathbb{R}^m 	o \mathbb{R}$ a $C^1$ function with $
abla P(x) \cdot x > w(
abla P(x))$ for $x 
otin C$, $P > 0$ off $C$ and $P = 0$ on $C$. If $z(t)$ solves (2.1), (C.3), (C.4), then $A(z(t)) 	o C$ as $t 	o \infty$.
nodes.statement_clean: Continuous-time generalized Blackwell approachability via a Lyapunov potential $\pi := P(A(z))$.
assumptions: $C \subset \mathbb{R}^m$ is closed, convex, and approachable: for every $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}^m$ there exists $\sigma^i \in \Delta(S^i)$ with $\lambda \cdot A(\sigma^i, s^{-i}) \le w(\lambda) := \sup\{\lambda \cdot y : y \in C\}$ for all $s^{-i}$
$P : \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}$ is $C^1$ with $\nabla P(x) \cdot x > w(\nabla P(x))$ off $C$, $P > 0$ off $C$, $P = 0$ on $C$
Player $i$ plays a generalized approachability strategy: $\lambda(t) \cdot A(q(t), s^{-i}) \le w(\lambda(t))$ with $\lambda(t) = \nabla P(A(z(t)))$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem C.1 (Lyapunov $\pi := P(A(z))$)
nodes.statement: Rescale $\dot z = q - z$. For $z \notin C$: $\dot \pi = \nabla P \cdot A(\dot z) = \lambda \cdot A(q^i, q^{-i}) - \lambda \cdot A(z) < w(\lambda) - w(\lambda) = 0$ by (C.4), (C.3), (C.2). $\pi$ is a strict Lyapunov function so $\pi \to 0$.
nodes.statement_clean: $\pi := P(A(z))$ is a strict Lyapunov function, mirroring the Blackwell argument.

nodes.name: Hannan's no-regret condition (cited)
nodes.statement: There exist play strategies achieving $u^i(z) \ge \max_{k} u^i(k, z^{-i})$ in the limit, the property defining the Hannan set.
nodes.statement_clean: Classical no-regret guarantee from Hannan 1957 motivating the Hannan set.

nodes.name: Discrete-time vanishing-regret theorem (cited)
nodes.statement: The discrete-time analog of Theorem 3.1: for the discrete $P^i$-strategy $q^i_k(T+1) = \widehat{\nabla} P^i_k(D^i(z_T))$, regrets vanish as $T \to \infty$.
nodes.statement_clean: Discrete-time precursor of Theorem 3.1.

nodes.name: Correlated equilibrium = non-positive conditional regret (cited)
nodes.statement: $z \in \Delta(S)$ is a correlated equilibrium iff $C^i(z) \le 0$ for all players $i$.
nodes.statement_clean: Characterization of correlated equilibria via conditional regrets, used to define the target set.

nodes.name: Blackwell's approachability theorem (cited)
nodes.statement: For a vector-payoff game with $A : S^i \times S^{-i} \to \mathbb{R}^m$ and a closed convex approachable set $C$, there exists a strategy of $i$ such that $A(z(t)) \to C$ as $t \to \infty$ (the original Blackwell strategy uses $P$ = squared Euclidean distance to $C$).
nodes.statement_clean: Classical Blackwell approachability for vector payoffs; Theorem C.1 generalizes it via potentials.

nodes.name: Azuma's inequality (cited)
nodes.statement: For martingale differences $Y_i$ with $|Y_i| \le K$: $\Pr[\sum_{i=1}^m Y_i > \lambda] < \exp(-\lambda^2/(2K^2 m))$.
nodes.statement_clean: Concentration inequality for bounded martingale differences, used in Step 5 of the Theorem A.1 proof.
